what: Show listening TCP/UDP sockets and the process that owns each one.
tip: Add -4 or -6 to limit the IP family. Needs root to see other users' processes.

what: Filesystem usage in human units, plus the filesystem type.
tip: First command for “disk full”. Follow with df -i to check inodes.

what: Size of each top-level directory, staying on one filesystem.
tip: -x stops du crossing into other mounts, so the numbers match df.

what: List open files that have been deleted (link count below 1).
tip: Explains why df shows full but du does not. Restart the holding process to free the space.

what: Block devices with filesystem type, label, UUID and mountpoint.
tip: Use it before touching any disk to confirm what is what.

what: Check /etc/fstab for mistakes without rebooting.
tip: Run it after every fstab edit. A bad entry can drop a server to emergency mode.

what: List every unit that failed since boot.
tip: A quick health check after a reboot or patching window.

what: Show errors and worse from the current boot.
tip: Add -u SERVICE to focus on one unit, or --since '1 hour ago'.

what: Five one-second samples of CPU, memory, swap and I/O.
tip: Read r (runnable), b (blocked), si/so (swap) and wa (I/O wait). Ignore the first line.

what: Per-device I/O: utilisation, latency (await) and queue size.
tip: From the sysstat package. High await with high %util means a saturated device.

what: Top memory consumers with their state and parent.
tip: Swap -%mem for -%cpu to rank by CPU.

what: Brief one-line-per-interface view of addresses and link state.
tip: Pair with ip route and ip -s link for counters.

what: Which interface, gateway and source IP would be used to reach an address.
tip: Great for debugging multi-homed servers and policy routing.

what: State of every NetworkManager-managed interface.
tip: Then nmcli connection show NAME for the full profile.

what: Print the SELinux mode: Enforcing, Permissive or Disabled.
tip: sestatus gives more detail, including the loaded policy.

what: Recent SELinux denials from the audit log.
tip: Pipe into audit2why to see a plain-language reason.

what: Reset SELinux file contexts to the policy default, verbosely.
tip: The fix for most “permission denied but modes look right” cases after moving files.

what: Logical volumes together with the physical devices they use.
tip: Shows at a glance which LV sits on which disk.

what: Multipath topology: maps, path groups and each path's state.
tip: Look for failed or faulty paths and the active/enabled grouping.

what: Kernel warnings and errors with human-readable timestamps.
tip: First stop for disk, NIC and driver problems.

what: Recent logins, reboots and shutdowns.
tip: Answers “when did this server last reboot, and who was on?”.

what: Password aging details for an account.
tip: Shows expiry, last change and the warning window.

what: Syntax-check sudoers files without opening an editor.
tip: A broken sudoers locks you out of sudo; always check after edits.

what: Test sshd_config for errors before restarting the daemon.
tip: Prevents locking yourself out over SSH.

what: List the start of an archive without extracting.
tip: Use -tjf for .bz2 and -tJf for .xz.

what: Copy a directory tree preserving permissions and times, with progress.
tip: A trailing slash on SRC copies its contents, not the directory itself. Add -n for a dry run.

what: Re-run a command every two seconds and show the output in place.
tip: Handy while a log or backup is growing.

what: See the resource limits (open files, processes) applied to one process.
tip: More accurate than ulimit -a, which shows only your shell.

what: Summarise the system calls a running process makes (Ctrl-C to stop).
tip: Add -f to follow children. Expect overhead; use briefly on busy production processes.

what: List units by how long they took to start at boot.
tip: Pair with systemd-analyze critical-chain.

what: How far the clock is from its time source and how it is being corrected.
tip: Large offsets break Kerberos, TLS and log correlation.

what: Memory and swap usage. Read the “available” column.
tip: “free” being small is normal on Linux; the kernel uses spare RAM for cache.

what: Uptime and the 1, 5 and 15-minute load averages.
tip: Compare load with nproc. Load above the CPU count means tasks are waiting.
